Spotify Music Popularity Analysis¶

Project Overview¶

This project analyzes Spotify track data to investigate which musical characteristics are most associated with song popularity. The analysis combines exploratory data analysis, unsupervised clustering, and classification modeling to examine patterns across genre and continuous audio features including danceability, energy, loudness, tempo, key, and duration.

Objective¶

The primary objective is to classify whether a track reaches a defined popularity threshold and identify which features contribute most strongly to differences between more- and less-popular songs.

Analytical Approach¶

The project includes:

  • Data cleaning and feature preparation
  • Exploratory analysis of track characteristics and popularity
  • Visualization of relationships among continuous and categorical variables
  • KMeans clustering to identify groups of tracks with similar audio characteristics
  • Classification modeling and model evaluation
  • Comparison of findings across EDA, clustering, and predictive modeling

Tools & Methods¶

Python • Pandas • Matplotlib • Seaborn • scikit-learn • Logistic Regression • KMeans Clustering • PCA

Methods include data cleaning, feature engineering, exploratory data analysis, correlation analysis, feature standardization, cluster evaluation, principal component analysis, categorical encoding, pipeline construction, stratified cross-validation, classification evaluation, and model interpretation.

Key Findings¶

Genre showed the strongest relationship with whether a track reached the primary popularity threshold. Among the continuous variables, energy and loudness were strongly related to one another, and higher values of both were more commonly associated with popular tracks. These patterns appeared consistently across exploratory analysis, clustering, and predictive modeling.

Data Cleaning¶

Initial inspection identified a small number of missing values in track-related fields. Missing records and duplicate tracks were removed before preparing the dataset for analysis.

In [8]:
df.dropna(axis = 0, how = 'any', inplace = True, ignore_index = False)
In [9]:
df.drop_duplicates(subset = ['track_id'],keep = 'first', inplace = True, ignore_index = False)
In [10]:
df['duration_min'] = (df['duration_ms'] // 60000) + (df['duration_ms'] % 60000) / 60000
In [11]:
df['key'] = df['key'].astype('category')

Popularity Thresholds¶

The original exploratory analysis categorized popularity using quartiles. For the classification analysis, I replaced that approach with three binary popularity thresholds at scores greater than 50, 60, and 70.

Using multiple thresholds allowed the analysis to compare whether relationships between track characteristics and popularity remained consistent as the definition of a popular track became more selective.

In [12]:
df['track_pop_50'] = np.where(df.track_popularity > 50, 1, 0)
In [13]:
df['track_pop_60'] = np.where(df.track_popularity > 60, 1, 0)
In [14]:
df['track_pop_70'] = np.where(df.track_popularity > 70, 1, 0)

Popularity Threshold Model Comparison¶

A preliminary logistic regression model was used to compare the three candidate popularity thresholds using the continuous audio features. Confusion matrices show how each threshold performs as a binary classification problem, while ROC curves compare the model's ability to distinguish between the two classes.

This comparison helps evaluate which popularity threshold is most appropriate for the more detailed modeling that follows.

In [29]:
# Compare preliminary classification performance across the three popularity thresholds

outcomes = ['track_pop_50', 'track_pop_60', 'track_pop_70']

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize = (13, 4))
fig_roc, ax_roc = plt.subplots(figsize = (7, 5))

for i, outcome in enumerate(outcomes):

    X = df[continuous_features]
    y = df[outcome]

    # Use the same train/test split for each popularity threshold

    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size = 0.25, random_state = 113)

    # Fit preliminary logistic regression model

    model = LogisticRegression(max_iter = 500)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)

    y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
    y_prob = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

    # Confusion matrix

    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)

    sns.heatmap(cm, annot = True, fmt = 'd', cbar = False, ax = ax[i])

    ax[i].set_title(outcome.replace('track_pop_', 'Popularity > '))
    ax[i].set_xlabel('Predicted Class')
    ax[i].set_ylabel('Actual Class')

    # ROC curve and AUC

    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, y_prob)
    roc_auc = auc(fpr, tpr)

    ax_roc.plot(fpr, tpr,
                label = f'{outcome.replace("track_pop_", "> ")} (AUC = {roc_auc:.3f})')

# Add reference line for random classification

ax_roc.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], '--')
ax_roc.set_title('ROC Curves by Popularity Threshold')
ax_roc.set_xlabel('False Positive Rate')
ax_roc.set_ylabel('True Positive Rate')
ax_roc.legend()

fig.tight_layout()
fig_roc.tight_layout()

plt.show()

The classification results reinforce the class-balance differences identified earlier. The greater-than-60 and greater-than-70 targets become increasingly difficult to classify, with the preliminary models predicting very few or no positive cases at the higher thresholds.

The greater-than-50 target provides a substantially more workable class distribution and was therefore selected as the outcome for the more detailed classification modeling later in the analysis.

Clustering Analysis¶

KMeans clustering was used to identify groups of tracks with similar continuous audio characteristics. The analysis uses danceability, loudness, energy, tempo, and duration.

In [30]:
# Create the dataset used for clustering

df_cluster = df[['danceability', 'loudness', 'energy',
                 'tempo', 'duration_min']].copy()

# Transform tempo and duration based on their observed distributions

df_cluster['tempo'] = np.log1p(df_cluster['tempo'])
df_cluster['duration_min'] = np.log1p(df_cluster['duration_min'])

# Standardize features so each variable contributes on a comparable scale

X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df_cluster)
In [31]:
# Confirm the clustering features are on comparable scales

df_scaled = pd.DataFrame(X, columns = df_cluster.columns)

sns.catplot(data = df_scaled, kind = 'box', aspect = 2)

plt.title('Standardized Features Used for Clustering')
plt.show()
In [32]:
# Compare within-cluster variation across possible values of k

tots_within = []
K = range(1, 31)

for k in K:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters = k, random_state = 113,
                n_init = 25, max_iter = 500)

    km.fit(X)
    tots_within.append(km.inertia_)

# Plot the elbow curve

fig, ax = plt.subplots()

ax.plot(K, tots_within, 'bo-')
ax.set_xlabel('Number of Clusters')
ax.set_ylabel('Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares')
ax.set_title('KMeans Elbow Method')

plt.show()
In [33]:
# Compare cluster separation for several possible values of k

silhouette_scores = []
K_test = range(2, 9)

for k in K_test:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters = k, random_state = 113,
                n_init = 25, max_iter = 500)

    cluster_labels = km.fit_predict(X)
    silhouette_scores.append(silhouette_score(X, cluster_labels))

# Display the silhouette score for each value of k

silhouette_results = pd.DataFrame({
    'Clusters': list(K_test),
    'Silhouette Score': silhouette_scores
})

silhouette_results

Cluster Selection¶

Silhouette analysis produced the highest score for a two-cluster solution, although overall silhouette values indicated substantial overlap among tracks.

Although the two-cluster solution produced the highest silhouette score, it separated tracks primarily into broad audio profiles with almost identical observed popularity rates. A four-cluster solution was retained as a more granular exploratory segmentation because it produced more distinct audio profiles and a wider range of observed popularity rates.

The four-cluster solution is therefore used for interpretation rather than presented as the mathematically optimal clustering solution.

In [36]:
# Fit the final four-cluster KMeans solution

cluster_4 = KMeans(n_clusters = 4, random_state = 113,
                   n_init = 25, max_iter = 500)

cluster_labels = cluster_4.fit_predict(X)

# Add cluster assignments to the original analysis data

df_cluster_final = df[continuous_features + 
                      ['track_popularity', 'track_pop_50']].copy()

df_cluster_final['cluster'] = cluster_labels

cluster_summary['popular_rate'] = cluster_summary['popular_rate'] * 100

Cluster Interpretation¶

The four-cluster solution identified distinct combinations of audio characteristics with different observed popularity rates.

Cluster 2 contained the most danceable tracks and relatively high energy and loudness, and had the highest proportion of tracks above the popularity threshold at approximately 41.7%. Cluster 1 contained the longest tracks and had the lowest popularity rate at approximately 29.0%.

The differences across clusters support the broader finding that combinations of audio characteristics are associated with popularity, while also showing that no single cluster profile determines whether a track will be popular.

Cluster Visualization with PCA¶

Principal component analysis was used to reduce the standardized clustering features to two dimensions so the four-cluster solution could be visualized more easily.

In [39]:
# Reduce the standardized clustering data to two dimensions for visualization

pca = PCA(n_components = 2)
pca_values = pca.fit_transform(X)

pca_df = pd.DataFrame(pca_values, columns = ['PC1', 'PC2'])
pca_df['cluster'] = cluster_labels

# Visualize the four audio clusters

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize = (8, 6))

sns.scatterplot(data = pca_df, x = 'PC1', y = 'PC2',
                hue = 'cluster', alpha = 0.5, ax = ax)

ax.set_title('Four-Cluster Solution Using PCA')
ax.set_xlabel('Principal Component 1')
ax.set_ylabel('Principal Component 2')

plt.show()

The PCA visualization shows substantial overlap among the tracks, which is consistent with the relatively low silhouette scores. The clusters therefore represent broad audio profiles rather than sharply separated groups.

Classification Modeling¶

The exploratory and clustering analyses showed that track characteristics contain some information related to popularity, but no individual feature cleanly separates popular from less-popular tracks.

The classification analysis therefore combines continuous audio features with playlist genre and musical key to predict whether a track has a popularity score greater than 50.

In [40]:
# Define the features and classification target

categorical_features = ['playlist_genre', 'key']
model_features = continuous_features + categorical_features

X_model = df[model_features]
y = df['track_pop_50']

# Create a stratified train/test split to preserve the outcome distribution

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_model, y, test_size = 0.25, random_state = 113,
    stratify = y)

print('Training observations:', len(X_train))
print('Testing observations:', len(X_test))

Training observations: 21264
Testing observations: 7088

Model Preprocessing¶

Continuous features are standardized before modeling, while the categorical variables are converted to indicator variables using one-hot encoding. A scikit-learn pipeline keeps preprocessing and model fitting together so the same transformations are applied consistently during training, validation, and prediction.

In [41]:
# Prepare continuous and categorical features for modeling

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(transformers = [
    ('continuous', StandardScaler(), continuous_features),
    ('categorical', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown = 'ignore',
                                  drop = 'first'), categorical_features)
])

# Create the logistic regression pipeline

full_model = Pipeline(steps = [
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', LogisticRegression(max_iter = 1000))
])

Model Comparison¶

Two logistic regression models were compared using stratified five-fold cross-validation. The first model uses only the continuous audio features, while the second adds playlist genre and musical key.

ROC AUC and accuracy are used to compare their ability to classify tracks above the popularity threshold.

In [42]:
# Create a model using only the continuous audio features

continuous_model = Pipeline(steps = [
    ('scaler', StandardScaler()),
    ('classifier', LogisticRegression(max_iter = 1000))
])

# Use stratified cross-validation because the classification outcome is imbalanced

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits = 5, shuffle = True, random_state = 113)

# Evaluate the continuous-only model

continuous_auc = cross_val_score(
    continuous_model, X_train[continuous_features], y_train,
    cv = cv, scoring = 'roc_auc')

continuous_accuracy = cross_val_score(
    continuous_model, X_train[continuous_features], y_train,
    cv = cv, scoring = 'accuracy')

# Evaluate the model containing continuous and categorical features

full_auc = cross_val_score(
    full_model, X_train, y_train,
    cv = cv, scoring = 'roc_auc')

full_accuracy = cross_val_score(
    full_model, X_train, y_train,
    cv = cv, scoring = 'accuracy')
In [43]:
# Summarize cross-validation performance

model_comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    'Model': ['Continuous Features', 'Continuous + Categorical'],
    'Mean Accuracy': [continuous_accuracy.mean(), full_accuracy.mean()],
    'Mean ROC AUC': [continuous_auc.mean(), full_auc.mean()]
})

model_comparison.round(3)

Model Mean Accuracy Mean ROC AUC
0 Continuous Features 0.631 0.603
1 Continuous + Categorical 0.644 0.659

Model Comparison Findings¶

Adding the categorical features improved model performance compared with using the continuous audio features alone.

Mean accuracy increased from 0.631 to 0.644, while mean ROC AUC increased from 0.603 to 0.659. The larger improvement in ROC AUC suggests that playlist genre and musical key add useful information for distinguishing between tracks above and below the popularity threshold.

The improvement is meaningful but still modest, indicating that popularity is only partially explained by the available audio and categorical features.

Final Logistic Regression Model¶

The full logistic regression model combines the continuous audio characteristics with playlist genre and musical key. The model is trained on the training data and evaluated using the held-out test set.

In [44]:
# Fit the final model

final_model = full_model
final_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Generate class predictions and predicted probabilities

y_pred = final_model.predict(X_test)
y_prob = final_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
In [45]:
# Evaluate final model performance on the held-out test set

model_results = pd.DataFrame({
    'Metric': ['Accuracy', 'Precision', 'Recall', 'F1 Score', 'ROC AUC'],
    'Score': [
        accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),
        precision_score(y_test, y_pred),
        recall_score(y_test, y_pred),
        f1_score(y_test, y_pred),
        roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob)
    ]
})

Test-Set Performance¶

The final model achieved an accuracy of 0.649 and a ROC AUC of 0.663 on the held-out test set, indicating modest ability to distinguish between tracks above and below the popularity threshold.

Precision was 0.563, while recall was considerably lower at 0.242. At the default classification threshold of 0.50, the model therefore identifies only a portion of the tracks that actually exceed the popularity threshold.

These results reinforce that the available track characteristics contain useful predictive information, but are not sufficient for high-confidence classification of song popularity.

Confusion Matrix and ROC Curve¶

ax[0].set_ylabel('Actual Class')

ax[1].set_ylabel('True Positive Rate')
ax[1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The confusion matrix shows the model's classification results at the default probability threshold of 0.50, while the ROC curve evaluates discrimination across all possible classification thresholds.

Because the audio features overlap substantially between popularity classes, the model should be interpreted as identifying patterns associated with popularity rather than providing a deterministic prediction of whether a song will become popular.

Model Interpretation¶

Logistic regression coefficients were examined to identify which features have the strongest relationships with the predicted probability that a track exceeds the popularity threshold.

Because the continuous variables were standardized before modeling, their coefficients represent changes on a comparable standardized scale. Categorical coefficients represent differences relative to the reference category created during one-hot encoding.

In [47]:
# Retrieve the feature names created during preprocessing

feature_names = final_model.named_steps['preprocessor'].get_feature_names_out()

# Retrieve the fitted logistic regression coefficients

coefficients = final_model.named_steps['classifier'].coef_[0]

coefficient_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Feature': feature_names,
    'Coefficient': coefficients
})

# Clean the feature names created by the preprocessing pipeline

coefficient_df['Feature'] = (
    coefficient_df['Feature']
    .str.replace('continuous__', '', regex = False)
    .str.replace('categorical__', '', regex = False)
)

# Rank features by the size of their model coefficient

coefficient_df['Absolute Coefficient'] = coefficient_df['Coefficient'].abs()

top_coefficients = (
    coefficient_df
    .sort_values('Absolute Coefficient', ascending = False)
    .head(15)
)

top_coefficients[['Feature', 'Coefficient']].round(3)

Model Findings¶

Playlist genre produced the largest coefficients in the final logistic regression model. Rock, pop, Latin, rap, and R&B all showed strong positive relationships with the probability that a track exceeded the popularity threshold relative to the model's reference genre.

Among the continuous audio features, loudness had a positive coefficient while energy had a negative coefficient after controlling for the other variables in the model. Because energy and loudness are strongly correlated, these coefficients should be interpreted as their individual relationships with popularity while the other model features are held constant rather than as simple standalone effects.

Musical key, danceability, tempo, and duration produced comparatively smaller coefficients. Overall, the model reinforces the earlier exploratory finding that genre contributes substantial predictive information, while individual audio characteristics provide additional but more limited separation between popular and less-popular tracks.

The coefficients describe associations within this dataset and should not be interpreted as evidence that any particular genre or audio characteristic causes a song to become popular.

Final Findings¶

The analysis identified several consistent patterns across exploratory analysis, clustering, and classification modeling.

  • Playlist genre showed substantial differences in observed popularity rates and emerged as an important source of predictive information.
  • Energy and loudness had the strongest relationship among the continuous audio features and repeatedly appeared together across exploratory and clustering analysis.
  • In the exploratory analysis, higher energy and loudness values were more commonly associated with tracks above the popularity threshold, although neither feature alone clearly separated the two popularity classes.
  • A four-cluster solution produced distinct audio profiles with observed popularity rates ranging from approximately 29.0% to 41.7%.
  • Classification modeling showed that track characteristics provide useful information about popularity, but substantial overlap remains between popular and less-popular tracks.

Overall, song popularity is associated with combinations of genre and audio characteristics rather than any single measurable feature. These relationships are observational and should not be interpreted as evidence that particular audio characteristics cause a song to become popular.

Data Source¶

The Spotify track dataset used in this analysis is available through the R for Data Science TidyTuesday Spotify Songs dataset.

The notebook retrieves the source data directly from the public repository so the analysis can be reproduced without requiring a separate local data file.
